articles.title: PM pledges continued support for Ukraine ahead of Zelensky visit
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president will be Andy Burnham's first international visitor since taking office.
articles.content:
Andy Burnham has pledged to continue the UK's "unwavering" support for Ukraine ahead of meeting Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.

The Ukrainian president will become the prime minister's first international visitor since he took office a week ago, which No 10 said "illustrates the strength of the relationship between the two nations".

They will visit a naval base, where Burnham will announce the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.

Burnham told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the visit that he was looking forward to it and that his support for Ukraine was "unwavering - it is 100%".

The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to.

The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.

Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.

It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.

Burnham said in a statement on Sunday evening: "Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries."

During Monday's visit, the two leaders will also meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.

Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and tangible support action involving the sharing of advanced electronic warfare technology ('Stone Cloak') from the UK to Ukraine, which has broad implications for security and defense capabilities. This transfer of technology represents a meaningful international collaboration with real-world impact on military defense and security, benefiting not only Ukraine but also contributing to the UK's future defense systems. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights innovation with large-scale benefits.

articles.title: Hidden genetic diversity helped inbred brown tree snakes conquer guam
articles.summary: A notorious snake invasion that devastated Guam’s native birds may have succeeded because the reptiles carried hidden genetic advantages. Using advanced long-read DNA sequencing, researchers uncovered more than 19,000 large genetic differences in brown tree snakes, many concentrated in genes tied to immunity and smell. This overlooked diversity may have helped a population founded by only a few snakes survive inbreeding, adapt to a new environment, and multiply to extraordinary densities.
articles.content:
The brown tree snake has become one of the world's best-known examples of an invasive species.

Native to Australia and the South Pacific, the snake likely reached Guam sometime after World War II, possibly by hiding aboard military cargo planes. Its arrival had devastating consequences. Brown tree snakes have driven many of Guam's native forest birds to local extinction, and they cause hundreds of power outages each year by climbing utility poles and electrical equipment.

In some parts of the U.S. territory, their numbers have climbed as high as 30,000 snakes per square mile.

A Snake Invasion That Defied Expectations

The invasion has long puzzled biologists because Guam's population is believed to have begun with only a small number of snakes.

Such a limited founding population usually creates a severe genetic bottleneck. With fewer genetic differences to draw upon, inbreeding would normally reduce a species' ability to adapt and make rapid population growth less likely.

A new University at Buffalo-led study, published on July 24 in Science Advances, suggests that brown tree snakes possess far more genetic variation than scientists previously recognized.

Researchers from UB and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) used advanced long-read sequencing to examine large sections of the snake's genome. They uncovered thousands of structural variants, including DNA segments that had been duplicated, deleted, or rearranged.

Many of these variations were concentrated in genes related to immunity and smell.

This hidden genetic diversity may help explain how a population founded by only a handful of snakes survived intense inbreeding, adapted to Guam, and expanded so dramatically.

"The brown tree snake is maybe not wildly diverse, but it has important sources of genetic diversity that have been underappreciated," says the study's corresponding author, Trevor Krabbenhoft, PhD, associate professor in the UB Department of Biological Sciences.

Findings With Implications Beyond Guam

The discovery may be discouraging for agencies that have spent decades trying to contain Guam's brown tree snake population. Greater genetic flexibility could make the invasive species more resilient than previously assumed.

At the same time, the results may offer hope for endangered species with small or highly inbred populations.

"It's possible that endangered species may have more flexibility in their genes than we realize," says first author Christopher Osborne, PhD, a former PhD student in Krabbenhoft's lab and now an aquatic biologist with State University of New York Oswego. "We're now getting a better understanding of unappreciated sources of genetic diversity that may explain how some inbred species can still respond to their environment."

Long-Read Sequencing Reveals Hidden DNA Changes

Much of what scientists know about genetic diversity has come from studying changes in individual DNA base pairs, such as an A changing to a G or a T changing to a C.

Early DNA sequencing tools were designed primarily to detect these small changes. They were much less effective at identifying major differences involving longer stretches of DNA.

Long-read sequencing allows researchers to examine much larger, continuous pieces of a genome. This makes it possible to detect structural variants that affect 50 base pairs or more.

Taken together, structural variants alter nearly eight times more of the genome than changes involving single base pairs.

"It's like looking at portions of two books letter by letter with a magnifying glass and thinking they're the same, but not realizing entire paragraphs have been moved around or duplicated. Older sequencing technology didn't allow us to easily see that DNA in one individual might be in a completely different place on the chromosome than in another," says Levi Gray, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher in Krabbenhoft's lab. "How we define genetic diversity and how we actually measure it is shaped largely by the technology of the day."

Gray previously studied Guam's brown tree snake problem while working for the USGS. Through that collaboration, the researchers obtained DNA from the USGS Brown Tree Snake Rapid Response Team (RRT), which works to prevent the invasive species from spreading elsewhere in the U.S. and its territories.

More Than 19,000 Structural Variants

When the team analyzed the samples in Krabbenhoft's laboratory, they identified more than 19,000 structural variants in the brown tree snake genome.

That means the researchers found roughly 19,000 locations where sections of DNA differed because they had been duplicated, deleted, or rearranged.

These variations were not scattered randomly throughout the genome. Instead, they appeared especially often in genes involved in immune function and olfaction, or the sense of smell.

Brown tree snakes depend heavily on smell to navigate and hunt. By flicking their forked tongues, they collect chemical signals from the air that help them locate potential prey.

The unusual diversity found in their olfactory genes could also help explain a behavioral mystery. Brown tree snakes are known to eat other snakes in their native range, but there is little evidence that they frequently prey on one another in Guam.

"The snakes' heightened sense of smell may allow them to recognize one another as something more like siblings -- especially given the high levels of inbreeding -- than as prey," Gray says.

Did the Genetic Diversity Emerge on Guam?

Scientists still do not know whether the structural variants were already present before the snakes reached Guam or whether some appeared after the invasion began.

Large genomic changes usually build up over many generations. However, some research suggests that severe population bottlenecks may accelerate the development of structural variants.

Determining when these changes appeared will require comparisons with brown tree snakes from their native range.

"Is it possible some of this diversity emerged after the invasion? It is, but we would have to sequence snakes from the native populations to know for sure," Gray says.

Other co-authors include USGS scientists M. Renee Bellinger, PhD, and Melia Nafus, PhD, as well as UB research scientist Brian Foote, postdoctoral researcher Steven Fleck, PhD, and PhD students Sarah Chang and Hannah Waterman.

This breakthrough improves understanding of genetic adaptation and resilience, with broad implications for conservation biology and endangered species management, thus having meaningful real-world impact beyond a niche audience.
articles.personality_title: Hidden genetic diversity helped invasive brown tree snakes thrive on Guam
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Brown tree snakes are native to Australia and the South Pacific. After World War II, a few snakes likely arrived on Guam, an island in the Pacific, and caused major harm by killing many native birds and disrupting power lines. Usually, when a small number of animals start a new population, they have less genetic variety, which makes it harder to survive and grow.

**What happened** – Scientists from the University at Buffalo and the U.S. Geological Survey used a new method called long-read DNA sequencing to study the snakes’ genes. They found over 19,000 big genetic differences, especially in genes related to the snakes’ immune system and sense of smell. This hidden variety may have helped the small group of snakes survive inbreeding, adapt to Guam’s environment, and multiply quickly.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that the snakes have more genetic strength than previously thought. It explains how they became so successful on Guam despite starting from few individuals. It also changes how scientists understand genetic diversity because older methods missed these large DNA changes. The findings might help conservation efforts by showing that endangered animals with small populations could have hidden genetic advantages too.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to compare the Guam snakes’ genes to those of snakes from their original homes. This will help find out if the genetic diversity was already there or developed after arriving on Guam. Understanding this could improve ways to control invasive species and protect endangered ones.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Advanced DNA analysis revealed unexpected genetic variety in Guam’s invasive brown tree snakes, helping explain their survival and rapid growth from a small starting group.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une diversité génétique cachée a aidé les serpents arboricoles envahissants à prospérer à Guam
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les serpents arboricoles sont originaires d’Australie et du Pacifique Sud. Après la Seconde Guerre mondiale, quelques serpents ont probablement atteint Guam, une île du Pacifique, où ils ont causé de grands dégâts en tuant de nombreux oiseaux natifs et en perturbant les lignes électriques. Habituellement, lorsqu’un petit nombre d’animaux fonde une nouvelle population, la diversité génétique est faible, ce qui complique leur survie et leur croissance.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques de l’Université de Buffalo et du Service géologique des États-Unis ont utilisé une nouvelle méthode appelée séquençage ADN à longue lecture pour étudier les gènes des serpents. Ils ont découvert plus de 19 000 grandes différences génétiques, surtout dans les gènes liés au système immunitaire et à l’odorat. Cette diversité cachée a peut-être aidé les serpents à survivre à la consanguinité, à s’adapter à l’environnement de Guam et à se multiplier rapidement.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que les serpents ont plus de force génétique qu’on ne le pensait. Elle explique leur succès à Guam malgré leur petit nombre initial. Elle change aussi la compréhension scientifique de la diversité génétique, car les méthodes plus anciennes manquaient ces grandes variations ADN. Ces résultats pourraient aider la conservation en montrant que les espèces en danger avec peu d’individus ont peut-être aussi des avantages génétiques cachés.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent comparer les gènes des serpents de Guam avec ceux des serpents de leur habitat d’origine. Cela permettra de savoir si la diversité génétique existait déjà ou est apparue après leur arrivée à Guam. Mieux comprendre cela pourrait améliorer la gestion des espèces envahissantes et la protection des espèces menacées.

**Une phrase clé** – Une analyse ADN avancée a révélé une diversité génétique inattendue chez les serpents arboricoles envahissants de Guam, expliquant leur survie et leur croissance rapide à partir d’un petit groupe initial.
articles.personality_title_es: La diversidad genética oculta ayudó a prosperar a las serpientes arborícolas invasoras en Guam
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las serpientes arborícolas son originarias de Australia y el Pacífico Sur. Después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, unas pocas serpientes llegaron probablemente a Guam, una isla en el Pacífico, donde causaron grandes daños al matar muchas aves nativas y afectar las líneas eléctricas. Normalmente, cuando un pequeño grupo de animales comienza una nueva población, tienen poca variedad genética, lo que dificulta su supervivencia y crecimiento.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos de la Universidad de Buffalo y del Servicio Geológico de EE. UU. usaron un nuevo método llamado secuenciación de ADN de lectura larga para estudiar los genes de las serpientes. Encontraron más de 19,000 diferencias genéticas grandes, especialmente en genes relacionados con el sistema inmunológico y el sentido del olfato. Esta diversidad oculta pudo haber ayudado a las serpientes a sobrevivir la endogamia, adaptarse al ambiente de Guam y multiplicarse rápidamente.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento muestra que las serpientes tienen más fuerza genética de la que se pensaba. Explica cómo lograron tener éxito en Guam a pesar de comenzar con pocos individuos. También cambia la forma en que los científicos entienden la diversidad genética, porque los métodos antiguos no detectaban estos grandes cambios en el ADN. Los resultados pueden ayudar en la conservación al mostrar que animales en peligro con poblaciones pequeñas podrían tener ventajas genéticas ocultas.

**Próximos pasos** – Los investigadores quieren comparar los genes de las serpientes de Guam con los de las serpientes de su lugar de origen. Esto ayudará a saber si la diversidad genética ya existía o apareció después de llegar a Guam. Entender esto podría mejorar el control de especies invasoras y la protección de especies en peligro.

**Una frase clave** – Un análisis avanzado de ADN reveló una variedad genética inesperada en las serpientes arborícolas invasoras de Guam, ayudando a explicar su supervivencia y rápido crecimiento desde un pequeño grupo inicial.
